summary: Define the compositum as the smallest field containing several subfields of a common overfield. Express elements of finitely generated extensions as rational functions and compute compositum degrees in concrete examples.
keyPoints: For $E,F\subset L$, the compositum $EF$ is the smallest subfield of $L$ containing both $E$ and $F$.
Every element of $F(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ is a quotient of polynomials in the $\alpha_i$, with nonzero denominator.
Several generators can sometimes be combined into one, as in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)$.

summary: Organize the behavior of field extensions in towers and composita through a common framework. Verify that finite extensions and algebraic extensions satisfy the required stability properties.
keyPoints: A distinguished class satisfies stability conditions for towers, extension of the base field, and composita.
For a tower $E/F/k$, the extension $E/k$ is finite if and only if both $E/F$ and $F/k$ are finite.
Compositions and composita of algebraic extensions are algebraic, and algebraicity is preserved under extension of the base field.

titleEn: Algebraically Closed Fields and Algebraic Closures
summary: Define an algebraically closed field as one with no nontrivial algebraic extensions. Study algebraic closures, embeddings of algebraic extensions, and uniqueness up to an isomorphism fixing the base field.
keyPoints: A field $F$ is algebraically closed if and only if every irreducible polynomial in $F[x]$ has degree $1$.
If $E/F$ is algebraic and $E$ is algebraically closed, then $E$ is an algebraic closure of $F$.
Every algebraic extension of $F$ embeds into an algebraic closure by an embedding fixing $F$, and any two algebraic closures are isomorphic over $F$.

summary: Construct a field by adjoining all roots of a polynomial so that it splits into linear factors. Establish the existence and finiteness of splitting fields and work through examples of low-degree polynomials.
keyPoints: A splitting field of $f\in F[x]$ is an extension generated by the roots of $f$ in which $f$ splits completely.
Every polynomial of positive degree has a splitting field, which is a finite extension of $F$.
The splitting field of $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]2,\zeta_3)$.

summary: Study algebraic extensions that contain all roots of an irreducible polynomial whenever they contain one root. Connect normality with splitting fields and embeddings into an algebraic closure.
keyPoints: If an algebraic extension $K/k$ is normal, every irreducible polynomial in $k[x]$ having a root in $K$ splits completely in $K[x]$.
Normality is equivalent both to $K$ being a splitting field of a family of polynomials in $k[x]$ and to every $k$-embedding $K\to\overline{k}$ having image $K$.
If $K/k$ is normal and $k\subset E\subset K$, then $K/E$ is normal; composita and intersections of normal extensions in a common overfield are also normal.

summary: Use formal derivatives to detect repeated roots and extend the notion of separability to elements and field extensions. Interpret separable degree as the number of distinct embeddings into an algebraic closure.
keyPoints: A nonzero polynomial $f$ is separable if and only if $\gcd(f,f')=1$.
For a finite extension $K/k$, the separable degree $[K:k]_s$ is the number of distinct $k$-embeddings $K\to\overline{k}$, and $[K:k]_s\le [K:k]$.
Separable degrees multiply in a tower of finite extensions $F/K/k$, and $F/k$ is separable if and only if both $F/K$ and $K/k$ are separable.

summary: Determine when a finite extension generated by several elements can be generated by a single element. Use multiplicative groups of finite fields and counts of embeddings to prove that every finite separable extension has a primitive element.
keyPoints: Every finite subgroup of the multiplicative group of a field is cyclic; in particular, $K^\times$ is cyclic for a finite field $K$.
Every finite extension of a finite field is simple, and more generally every finite separable extension is simple.
A finite extension $K/k$ is simple if and only if it has only finitely many intermediate fields.

summary: Construct finite fields as splitting fields and establish existence and uniqueness for each possible cardinality. Use the Frobenius automorphism to determine the automorphism groups of finite field extensions.
keyPoints: For each $q=p^n$, there is a field $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $q$ elements, unique up to isomorphism; it is the splitting field of $x^q-x$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$.
The extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}/\mathbb{F}_q$ is normal and separable of degree $m$.
The full automorphism group consists of the $m$ automorphisms $1,\sigma_q,\dots,\sigma_q^{m-1}$, where $\sigma_q(a)=a^q$.

titleEn: Purely Inseparable Extensions and Perfect Fields
summary: Analyze failures of separability in positive characteristic using powers and derivatives. Describe inseparable degree, purely inseparable extensions, and perfect fields to clarify when extensions are separable.
keyPoints: Irreducible polynomials over a field of characteristic $0$ are separable; in characteristic $p$, the condition $f'=0$ implies that $f(x)=g(x^p)$.
For a finite extension, $[K:k]_i=[K:k]/[K:k]_s$; in a purely inseparable extension of characteristic $p$, some $p$-power of each $\alpha$ lies in $k$.
A field of characteristic $p$ satisfying $k^p=k$ is called perfect, and every finite extension of a perfect field is separable.

summary: Define a Galois extension as a finite extension that is both normal and separable. Compute automorphisms of quadratic and cyclotomic extensions and examine the preservation of the Galois property under composita.
keyPoints: A finite extension $K/k$ is Galois if it is both normal and separable.
Quadratic extensions of fields of characteristic other than $2$ and cyclotomic extensions $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}$ are Galois.
We have $[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(n)$, and the automorphisms are determined by $\zeta_n\mapsto\zeta_n^t$ for integers $t$ with $(t,n)=1$.

titleEn: The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory
summary: Relate intermediate fields to subgroups of the Galois group through an inclusion-reversing correspondence. Prove the fundamental theorem using fixed fields and Artin's theorem, and interpret polynomial Galois groups as permutation groups.
keyPoints: For a finite Galois extension $K/k$, the maps $H\mapsto K^H$ and $E\mapsto\mathrm{Gal}(K/E)$ are mutually inverse, inclusion-reversing correspondences.
For a finite group $G$ of automorphisms of $K$, its fixed field satisfies $[K:K^G]=|G|$ and $\mathrm{Aut}(K/K^G)=G$.
The Galois group of a separable irreducible polynomial of degree $n$ acts faithfully and transitively on its roots, so it may be viewed as a transitive subgroup of $S_n$.

summary: View a finite extension as a vector space and define norm and trace through the determinant and trace of multiplication maps. Compute them as products and sums of conjugates and study trace duality for separable extensions.
keyPoints: For a finite extension $K/k$, let $m_\alpha(x)=\alpha x$; then $N_{K/k}(\alpha)=\det(m_\alpha)$ and $\mathrm{Tr}_{K/k}(\alpha)=\mathrm{tr}(m_\alpha)$.
The norm is the product of the $\sigma(\alpha)$ over distinct embeddings, raised to the power $[K:k]_i$; the trace is the corresponding sum multiplied by $[K:k]_i$.
For a finite separable extension, the trace is a nonzero linear map and $(x,y)\mapsto\mathrm{Tr}_{K/k}(xy)$ is a nondegenerate bilinear form.

titleEn: Applications of Galois Theory: Solvability by Radicals
summary: Connect towers formed by successively adjoining radicals with solvable Galois groups. Use the obstruction supplied by a nonsolvable Galois group to study examples of quintic equations that cannot be solved by radicals.
keyPoints: An extension generated by radicals is described by a finite tower $K_i=K_{i-1}(\alpha_i^{1/d_i})$, with each $d_i$ assumed invertible in the base field.
The Galois closure of such a radical extension has a solvable Galois group.
An irreducible polynomial in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ of prime degree $p\ge5$ with exactly two nonreal roots has Galois group $S_p$, so it is not solvable by radicals.

titleEn: Applications of Galois Theory: Straightedge and Compass Constructions
summary: Interpret coordinates obtained by straightedge and compass constructions through field operations and adjoining square roots. Use towers of quadratic extensions to study constructible regular polygons and the problem of doubling the cube.
keyPoints: The constructible real numbers form a field, and the square root of a positive constructible real number is also constructible.
A real algebraic number $\alpha$ is constructible if and only if $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ can be obtained through a tower of quadratic extensions.
For a prime $p=2^n+1$, the regular $p$-gon is constructible, whereas $\sqrt[3]2$ is not constructible because its degree is $3$.
